summary: This House resolution directs Congress to defund and replace ICE with a new DOJ agency under civilian oversight, repeal its $75 billion allocation, impeach DHS and DOJ leaders, end qualified immunity for its agents, mandate body cameras and use-of-force standards, and launch investigations into agent misconduct.

scores.thoughts: The resolution explicitly calls for voting against any new DHS funding and repealing the $75 billion multi-year allocation to ICE. These provisions directly aim to cut federal spending on immigration enforcement, aligning strongly with reduced government spending.
The bill contains no provisions related to tax policy, rates, or revenue measures.
No references to healthcare systems, coverage, or policy appear in the text.
While the bill addresses use-of-force standards for ICE agents, it does not engage with broader gun regulations or Second Amendment issues.

The resolution seeks to dismantle aggressive ICE practices, replace the agency, prohibit profiling and militarized operations, and impose strict oversight and human-rights standards on enforcement and detention. This directly pushes toward expanded protections and reduced enforcement intensity.
No content addresses reproductive rights or abortion policy.
The bill targets DHS and ICE, not Department of Defense or military spending.
No environmental or climate provisions are present.
The resolution does not address welfare programs, food assistance, or related entitlements.
No education-related measures are included.
No drug-policy or enforcement provisions appear.

The bill mandates ending qualified immunity for ICE agents, independent investigations and prosecutions of misconduct, uniform use-of-force standards, and body-camera requirements. These are explicit accountability and reform measures aimed at law-enforcement behavior.
No trade, tariff, or globalization provisions are present.
While spending cuts are proposed, the resolution does not frame them in terms of debt reduction or deficit policy.
No provisions address LGBTQ+ legal protections or rights.
The bill does not mention foreign aid.
No voting-access or election-integrity measures are included.
Body-camera and identification requirements for officers are mentioned, but these are narrow accountability tools rather than broader tech or privacy regulation.
No labor, union, or worker-protection provisions appear.
The resolution does not engage with religious exemptions or civil-rights balancing.
